prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "MICROSOFT CORP" (ticker MSFT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MSFT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Microsoft Corporation
markets: Server and database software (Windows Server, SQL Server)

mission.statement: to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more
mission.source: Microsoft company website and annual report
mission.plain: Make tools that help people and businesses get more done.

about.plain: Microsoft makes software that most offices and computers run on, like Windows, Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams. It also rents huge computer centres over the internet, called Azure, where other companies run their apps and AI. It sells the Copilot AI helper, owns LinkedIn and the Xbox games business, including Minecraft and Call of Duty.
about.customers: Mostly businesses and governments, plus people who buy Windows PCs, Microsoft 365 subscriptions and Xbox games.
about.everyday: If you have typed in Word, made a slideshow in PowerPoint or played Minecraft, you have used Microsoft's products.

money.plain: renting computing power and AI, plus Windows Server and SQL Server
Office apps, Teams, Outlook and Dynamics subscriptions
PC software, games, devices and search ads
job ads, recruiting tools and premium memberships
an AI helper sold as an add-on to Office and Windows

result.summary: Microsoft has a wide moat built on Windows and Office being the default tools of work, which creates high switching costs and lets it bundle new products like Teams, security and Copilot to over 400 million commercial Office users. Azure is the second-largest cloud and passed $100B of annual revenue in FY2026, growing 43% in the June 2026 quarter, helped by its OpenAI partnership. Its commercial backlog of $678B gives unusual visibility, though it relies heavily on OpenAI.

pricingPower.evidence: Microsoft raised consumer Microsoft 365 prices by $3 a month in 2025 when adding Copilot, raised commercial Microsoft 365 suite prices again from July 2026, and lifted Xbox Game Pass Ultimate to $29.99 in 2025; commercial seat counts and Office revenue kept growing, while Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats at about $30 per user per month.

moats.evidence: Microsoft, Windows, Office, Xbox and LinkedIn are among the best known technology brands, and it is trusted by governments and large companies for security and support.
Companies run on Excel files, Outlook, Teams, Active Directory/Entra identity and Azure workloads; moving thousands of employees and systems off them is costly and risky.
Office file formats and Teams benefit from everyone using the same tools, LinkedIn has over a billion members, and Windows has the largest base of apps and developers on the PC.
It spent about $116B of capex in FY2026 on data centres, one of very few companies able to build AI capacity at that scale, and spreads software costs over hundreds of millions of users.
Hyperscale cloud is effectively a three-player market (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) because the investment needed keeps new entrants out.
Microsoft is mostly the incumbent; its bundling of Teams and Copilot into Microsoft 365 counter-positions point-solution rivals like Slack and Zoom.
Decades of selling to and supporting large enterprises, with a huge sales and partner channel, are hard to copy, though its software engineering itself is not unique.
Its roughly 27% stake in OpenAI and rights to OpenAI models and IP, plus an exclusive Azure API arrangement, give it privileged access to leading AI models.

customers.evidence: Microsoft 365 and Azure renewals are very high, commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678B in June 2026 (up 84%), and Windows still runs about 70% of the world's desktops; Teams and Windows updates draw frequent user complaints, so satisfaction is high on dependence more than delight.

talent.evidence: Microsoft is one of the most sought-after tech employers and ranks highly in employer surveys such as Forbes' World's Best Employers; it has also hired top AI talent such as Mustafa Suleyman, though it cut more than 15,000 jobs in 2025.

product.evidence: Office and Windows are the industry standards, Azure is the number-two cloud with fast-growing AI services, and GitHub Copilot was the first widely used AI coding assistant; however, its own AI models trail OpenAI, Google and Anthropic and Copilot reviews are mixed.

competitors.name: Amazon (AWS)
competitors.note: cloud infrastructure and AI platforms (AWS vs Azure)

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google)
competitors.note: Google Cloud vs Azure, Workspace vs Microsoft 365, Gemini vs Copilot, Search vs Bing, Chrome OS vs Windows

competitors.name: Salesforce
competitors.note: CRM and business apps (Dynamics 365), Slack vs Teams, AI agents

competitors.name: Oracle
competitors.note: databases, cloud infrastructure for AI and business applications

competitors.name: OpenAI
competitors.note: ChatGPT Enterprise competes with Copilot, even though Microsoft is its largest investor and cloud partner

competitors.name: Apple
competitors.note: macOS vs Windows, Mac vs Surface and PC partners

competitors.name: ServiceNow
competitors.note: workflow automation and AI agents for enterprises

competitors.name: Anthropic
competitors.note: Claude models for enterprise and coding vs Copilot (also a partner on Azure and in Copilot)

competitors.name: Adobe
competitors.note: documents (Acrobat vs Office/Word) and creative AI

competitors.name: Palo Alto Networks
competitors.note: cybersecurity vs Microsoft Defender and Sentinel

competitors.name: IBM
competitors.note: hybrid cloud, enterprise AI and consulting

competitors.name: Sony Group
competitors.note: PlayStation vs Xbox consoles and games

competitors.name: Meta Platforms
competitors.note: AI models and assistants, Workplace tools and VR

threats: Heavy dependence on OpenAI, which now also buys compute from other clouds and sells ChatGPT Enterprise directly against Copilot
Very large AI capex (about $116B in FY2026) whose returns are unproven and which is pressuring gross margin
Copilot adoption and pricing may disappoint if AI assistants become cheap commodities or users prefer rival tools
Antitrust and regulatory scrutiny of bundling (EU Teams case), cloud licensing practices and the OpenAI relationship
Google Workspace and AI-native tools chipping away at Office, and AWS and Google Cloud competing on AI chips and price
Weakness in gaming (Xbox content and services revenue fell 10% in the June 2026 quarter) and in Windows OEM

ceo.name: Satya Nadella
ceo.background: electrical engineer (Manipal Institute of Technology), MS in computer science from the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, MBA from the University of Chicago Booth; previously ran Microsoft's cloud and server business

c1.evidence: Microsoft is a leader in AI infrastructure and enterprise AI, with Azure passing $100B of annual revenue in FY2026 and growing 43% in the June 2026 quarter.

c2.evidence: Businesses choose Microsoft because its tools are the standard, come in one bundle with security and identity, and are backed by a huge partner network; these switching costs have lasted for decades.

c3.evidence: Microsoft is a household name and the default for PC software and office work, with Windows on about 70% of desktops and Office used by over 400 million commercial seats.

c4.evidence: Nadella relaunched the mission 'to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more' in 2015 and repeats it often, but the company is run with a strong focus on profit and market share.

c6.evidence: “reliable, corporate, everywhere, Windows and Office” — the impression is mostly positive and trusted, though some see it as bureaucratic, and Windows and Teams draw complaints.

c7.evidence: It rides the cloud and AI secular trends, with commercial remaining performance obligation of $678B in June 2026, up 84% year on year.

c8.evidence: Its cloud and AI platform lets it expand into AI agents, security, healthcare AI (Nuance/Dragon Copilot), custom chips (Maia) and quantum computing (Majorana 1).

m1.evidence: Nadella moved Microsoft to 'mobile-first, cloud-first' in 2014 and bet early on OpenAI in 2019, positioning it to lead enterprise AI.

m2.evidence: Nadella is not a founder but a 30-year Microsoft veteran who invests for the long term, such as the multi-year OpenAI partnership and data-centre build-out.

m4.evidence: Nadella is known for empathy and a 'learn-it-all' growth mindset, and wrote 'Hit Refresh' about putting customers and employees first, though large layoffs in 2023 and 2025 cut against this.

m5.evidence: He deliberately replaced Microsoft's infighting culture with a growth-mindset culture, which helped produce Azure, Teams and GitHub Copilot.

m6.evidence: Nadella is an electrical engineer and computer scientist who ran Microsoft's server and cloud engineering before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: Nadella is widely respected for humility and empathy, shaped partly by caring for his son with cerebral palsy, and pushes accessibility and responsible AI.

m7b.evidence: I could not confirm that Nadella has given a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Nadella is calm, thoughtful and low-key rather than a flamboyant, larger-than-life personality.

m9.evidence: Under Nadella revenue grew from about $87B in FY2014 to $332B in FY2026 and the market value rose roughly tenfold, to around $4 trillion.

m10.evidence: Microsoft is not known for frugality and spends heavily on AI, but it keeps tight cost control, with operating margin rising to about 47% in FY2026.

c10.evidence: Windows, Office and Azure are used by over a billion people and most of the world's businesses, schools and governments to work and learn.

p2.evidence: Building global-scale cloud and AI infrastructure and operating systems used by billions is extremely hard and important to the world economy.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $168.1B in FY2021 to $331.8B in FY2026.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from about 42% in FY2021 to about 47% in FY2026, but gross margin slipped from about 69% to about 68% as AI infrastructure costs rose.

f3.evidence: At June 2026 it held $76.8B of cash and short-term investments against $40.3B of debt, with $182.9B of FY2026 operating cash flow and positive equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income grew from $69.9B in FY2021 to $155.2B in FY2026 and operating cash flow from $76.7B to $182.9B.

v1.evidence: Office and Windows are the standard because everyone else uses them, a reason ordinary people understand, but Azure, Copilot and Teams are not clearly best in class against AWS, ChatGPT or Google.

v2.evidence: Microsoft regularly ranks near the top of employer lists such as Forbes' World's Best Employers and LinkedIn Top Companies, helped by its culture turnaround under Nadella.

c5.evidence: If Microsoft disappeared overnight most offices, hospitals, schools and governments would lose their computers' operating system, email, documents and cloud services, causing global disruption.
